They invest in visibility (ads, social media, yard signs, sponsorships) and wonder why they are still competing on price against competitors with smaller budgets and thinner margins. The issue isn't that customers don't know they exist. The issue is that customers don't have a strong reason to choose them specifically. Being the local favorite is a different thing entirely from being locally known. The local favorite is the business people name when someone asks for a recommendation, before they are even asked for a category. It is the business people return to without comparing alternatives. It is the business whose customers become unpaid advocates, dropping the name in conversation, in Facebook groups, and in review responses that send more customers through the door. Being known means people are aware your business exists. Being the local favorite means people choose you first, recommend you without being asked, and return without comparing alternatives. The gap between the two is brand positioning , and most local businesses have never done it deliberately. What Makes Northern Indiana & Michiana Different Northern Indiana and Michiana ( Elkhart County , Goshen , Elkhart , Mishawaka , South Bend , and the communities surrounding them) is not a generic local market. It has a character that shapes how trust is built, how reputations travel, and what it actually takes to become the business people talk about. This is a manufacturing and trades heritage market. The RV industry alone makes Elkhart County one of the most industrially concentrated counties in the country. That heritage shapes customer values in ways that affect every local business, regardless of industry. Customers here respect reliability, straight talk, and demonstrable expertise over polished marketing. They are skeptical of businesses that feel like they are selling and loyal to businesses that feel like they are delivering. Word of mouth in this market travels fast and sticks long. A reputation built well compounds here. A reputation mismanaged is difficult to recover from. And the close-knit community structure means that showing up genuinely (in churches, in youth leagues, in chambers and community organizations) builds the kind of familiarity that advertising cannot buy. The Four Pillars of Local Favorite Status The businesses that become the local favorite in Northern Indiana and Michiana do four things consistently. Most local businesses do one or two of these sporadically. The gap between occasional and consistent is the gap between being occasionally mentioned and being the name everyone uses. Define Your Position Before You Market Anything The single most common mistake local businesses make is marketing before positioning. They build a website, run ads, post on social media, and because none of it is built on a clear strategic foundation, none of it compounds. Each piece of marketing is a standalone expense rather than a deposit into a building brand asset. Positioning answers three questions with precision: What specific problem do you solve, for whom specifically, and why is your approach different from every alternative available to them in this market? The geographic specificity matters here. "We serve small business owners in Elkhart County who are overwhelmed by financial complexity" is a positioning statement. The businesses that win their local markets do something fundamentally different: they build a brand that removes the need for the customer to compare at all. Brand positioning is the deliberate decision about what your business stands for in the minds of your local customers - the specific, ownable territory you occupy that makes you the obvious choice for a clearly defined audience with a clearly defined need. When positioning is done well, customers do not ask how much you charge before they ask whether you are available. They do not compare you to three other businesses before deciding. They call you because you are who they think of when they think of what they need. For local businesses, positioning has a geographic dimension that national brands cannot replicate. You can claim a specific community, a specific local expertise, and a specific relationship with the people and places in your market that no outsider can authentically match. That local specificity is the foundation on which the strongest local brands are built. 2. Category Design: Define the Game You Win The most powerful brand positioning strategy available to a local business is not to compete better within an existing category - it is to define a new category in which your business is the obvious leader. This concept, known as category design, shifts the competitive dynamic from "who is best" to "who is the only one doing this." The Category Design Principle Every market has categories that customers use to organize their choices. "Plumbers," "accountants," "real estate agents" - these are categories. Categories have implicit evaluation criteria: price, availability, reviews. When you compete within an existing category, you are playing by someone else's rules, and the customer's primary decision mechanism is comparison. When you define a new category, you write the rules. Instead of being the best plumber in Goshen, you become the home systems specialist for Northern Indiana families - the business that handles plumbing, HVAC, and electrical as an integrated system rather than three separate vendors. That is a different category with different evaluation criteria, and when you set the criteria, you win. The category design test: If a potential customer could describe your business in the same sentence they would use to describe your three closest competitors, you are in a commodity category. If describing what you do requires a sentence that only applies to you, you have begun the work of category design. Local Category Opportunities Local markets are full of category design opportunities precisely because most local businesses have never thought about this. The local accountant who becomes the tax strategist for Elkhart County manufacturers. The local gym that becomes the performance training center for Northern Indiana athletes over 40. The local insurance agency that becomes the risk management partner for Michiana family businesses. Each of these is a category that did not exist before the business claimed it - and in each case, the business that claims it first and builds a content and community presence around it is extraordinarily difficult to displace. 3. They write articles one by one, based on whatever idea pops into their head, and then wonder why their site doesn't rank despite having hundreds of posts. The issue is almost never the quality of individual articles: it's the lack of proper structure. Google doesn't rank individual pages alone. It considers the relationships between pages, how well a topic is covered, and the authority signals that come from a well-connected content structure. This forms the basis of what SEO professionals call topical authority , which has become a key ranking factor in Google's algorithm since the Helpful Content System updates of 2022 and 2023. HubSpot , one of the earliest and most documented adopters of the pillar-cluster model, reported that after restructuring their blog around topic clusters in 2017, their organic search traffic grew significantly and their ability to rank new content improved greatly. Semrush's 2024 State of Content Marketing Report, based on a survey of over 1,500 content marketers, found that websites with a defined content structure were significantly more likely to report strong organic results. The takeaway before writing a single article: architecture is not optional. It is the foundation on which every piece of content either gains value or remains isolated, producing nothing. The Three Levels of Content Hierarchy The structure that consistently delivers the best SEO results functions on three distinct levels. Each level has a specific role, format, and connection to the other two. The pillar page is an authoritative, comprehensive hub for an entire topic. It covers everything a reader needs to understand about a subject at a high level, touching on all major subtopics without becoming so detailed that it overwhelms. Moz defines a pillar page as a website page that covers all aspects of a topic in depth, with room to link out to other pages that explore subtopics more thoroughly. Pillar pages typically range from 3,000 to 5,500 words. Their ranking strength grows over time as cluster articles build authority and pass it upward through internal links. Cluster articles are the workhorses of a content strategy. Each one dives deep into a specific subtopic introduced but not fully covered in the pillar page. If the pillar page is the table of contents, each cluster article is a complete chapter. They target long-tail keywords, which according to Ahrefs make up 92 percent of all search queries. While these keywords have lower search volumes, they convert at higher rates because the searcher's intent is more specific. Each cluster article links back to the pillar page, and the pillar links to each cluster, creating the hub-and-spoke structure that signals topical authority to Google. Supporting content sits beneath cluster articles. These are highly specific pieces (usually 600 to 1,200 words) that answer a very particular question or target a narrow query too small to justify a full cluster article. Google's own documentation emphasizes that it evaluates whether a site demonstrates expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness across a topic. Supporting content fills the gaps cluster articles leave, captures specific question-based queries, and directs authority upward into the cluster articles above it. What Topical Authority Actually Means Topical authority isn't a single metric that Google publishes. What Content Repurposing Actually Means Content repurposing is the practice of taking one core idea and expressing it in multiple formats, for multiple audiences, across multiple platforms, without starting from scratch each time. The example: A 45-minute webinar contains 6,000 to 9,000 words of spoken content. If you upload it to YouTube and move on, you have used maybe 5% of its potential value. But extract the transcript and you have the raw material for a long-form blog post, a LinkedIn article, eight standalone social posts, an email sequence, case study pages, an FAQ page, and a 60-second Reel. Eleven distinct pieces of content from one hour of work. That is content repurposing. Not copying and pasting the same text everywhere. Translating one idea into the native language of every platform where your audience lives. Why Most Businesses Fail at This The first reason is that most people think about content creation as an event: you sit down, you make something, you publish it, you are done. Repurposing requires you to think about content creation as a system. A system has inputs, processes, and outputs. The input is your core idea. The process is extraction and reformatting. The output is a stream of assets that work for you continuously. The second reason is that people underestimate how different each platform actually is. LinkedIn rewards professional insight and personal storytelling. Instagram rewards visual clarity and emotional resonance. A blog rewards depth, structure, and keyword optimization. You cannot take a blog post and copy it into an Instagram caption and expect it to work. The third reason is that most businesses have no documented content process at all. Below your pillar content are cluster pieces: medium-length articles, videos, or episodes that each explore one sub-topic from your pillar in detail. Each cluster piece is valuable on its own, but it also links back to your pillar and to each other. This creates a web of related content that signals topical authority to search engines. At the base are content atoms: the smallest, most shareable units of your content: a single statistic, a one-sentence insight, a short quote, a quick tip, a provocative question. They post because they feel they should, because a competitor is doing it, or because someone on the team had an idea that week. The content goes up, gets a brief window of visibility, and then disappears into the feed, never to generate another lead or visitor again. This is the disposable content trap. And it is extraordinarily expensive when you account for the time, energy, and money that goes into producing content with a shelf life measured in hours. There is a better way. The businesses that understand it are generating traffic, leads, and sales from articles, videos, and resources they created two, three, or five years ago. They did not get lucky. They made a deliberate choice to invest in evergreen content , and that choice is now compounding in their favor every single month. What Evergreen Content Actually Is: and What Most Businesses Get Wrong The term gets used loosely, so let us be precise. Evergreen content is content that remains relevant, useful, and discoverable to your target customer regardless of when they encounter it. It answers questions that do not expire. It solves problems that persist. It addresses concerns your customer faces whether they read it today or three years from now. The key distinction: Evergreen is not a content type. It is a property of the underlying question your content addresses. A post titled "Our Top Social Media Predictions for Q3" expires. A post titled "How to Choose a Social Media Strategy When You Have No Budget and No Team" does not. The deeper insight is about problem permanence. Every market has problems structural to how it operates, and those structural problems generate stable, recurring demand for information. A small business will always struggle with cash flow. A first-time homebuyer will always be confused about the mortgage process. A new manager will always underestimate the complexity of giving difficult feedback. These are not temporary problems. They are baked into the experience of being that customer, at that stage. Your job is to map the structural problems of your customer's experience and build content around the questions those problems generate. That is the intellectual foundation of an evergreen content strategy. The Decay Rate Framework: How to Evaluate Any Topic Before You Create Before investing in a piece of content, apply a decay rate analysis. Ask how quickly the answer to the question your content addresses will change. Most businesses understand this at the extremes but struggle with the middle. The practical test: if you read this content eighteen months from now, would a reader know it was written eighteen months ago? If yes, the decay rate is too high for a pure evergreen investment. They evaluate it in the context of everything else on your domain, everything that links to it from other domains, and the behavioral signals of every person who has ever interacted with it. A piece of content live for two years, with links from twenty websites and thousands of readers, is almost impossible to displace by a competitor who just published something on the same topic last week, even if their content is technically better. Why Content Marketing for Local Business Is a Fundamentally Different Discipline Most content marketing frameworks are built around national or global brands with large teams, significant budgets, and the ability to play a long game measured in years before seeing meaningful commercial return. You know your customers by name, by history, by the specific circumstances that brought them to you. This is not a consolation prize for being small. It is a genuine content advantage that is impossible to manufacture at scale. A national insurance company can write a generic guide to homeowners insurance. A local independent insurance agency in a specific city can write a guide to homeowners insurance that accounts for specific flood zone designations in that market, the particular wildfire risk in the surrounding county, local building codes that affect reconstruction costs, and the specific carriers that actually write policies in that area. That content is more useful, more specific, and more trustworthy to a local buyer than anything a national brand can produce efficiently. The Trust Proximity Effect Trust works differently at the local level. A national brand earns trust through reputation and institutional stability. A local business earns trust through familiarity, personal relationship, and demonstrated investment in the community. Local content marketing is partly a relationship-building exercise - the content that works best combines genuine expertise with genuine community embeddedness. The Competitive Landscape Reality In most local markets, the content marketing bar is extraordinarily low. Most local businesses have no content strategy at all. The few that produce content typically produce generic, templated material that reads as if it was written for any business in any city. A local business that commits to a genuine, strategic, community-rooted content program can dominate its local content landscape with a fraction of the investment required to compete nationally. 2. b: 01 What "Trust" Actually Means in Google's Context 02 The Foundation: E-E-A-T 03 Signal One: Backlinks From Authoritative Sources 04 Signal Two: Content Quality, Depth, and Accuracy 05 Signal Three: Technical Performance & Core Web Vitals 06 Signal Four: Demonstrated Authorship and Expertise 07 Signal Five: User Behavior Signals 08 Signal Six: Website Transparency 09 Signal Seven: Domain Age, History, and Consistency 10 Signal Eight: Internal Structure and Site Architecture 11 What Destroys Google's Trust 12 Trust Compounds Over Time What "Trust" Actually Means in Google's Context The term trust is often used loosely in SEO discussions, but Google doesn't use a single "trust score" for websites. Instead, it relies on a complex, multi-layered system of signals that collectively evaluate a website's content, authority, and reliability. When SEO experts say Google "trusts" a site, they mean it ranks the site favorably, crawls it often, boosts the ranking of new content, and recovers quickly from algorithm updates, more than sites lacking those signals. Understanding what builds and what destroys trust is essential for any business investing in search visibility . These signals include technical performance, content quality, external reputation, and user behavior. None work alone: they work together, and consistently high-ranking sites are those that have invested in all of them over time. The most important framework for understanding what Google values in a website is E-E-A-T : Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. This framework comes directly from Google's Search Quality Evaluator Guidelines: the document Google uses to train human quality raters who assess search results. Signal One: Backlinks From Authoritative, Relevant Sources Backlinks remain one of the most well-documented and consistently validated ranking signals in SEO research. Google's original PageRank algorithm was based on the idea that a link from one website to another is like a vote of confidence, and the authority of the linking site influences the strength of that vote. Backlinko's analysis of one billion pages revealed that the number of unique domains linking to a page was the most strongly correlated factor with first-page Google rankings. Pages with more unique linking domains consistently outranked pages with fewer, across almost every keyword category studied. Quality over quantity: A single backlink from a highly authoritative, topically relevant website carries more weight than hundreds of links from low-authority or unrelated sites. Ahrefs' research consistently shows that links from topically relevant sites, those covering the same subject area as the linked page, generate stronger ranking signals than links from unrelated domains. The practical takeaway: earning links through genuine value (publishing research others want to reference, creating tools people find useful, producing authoritative content that is cited) ultimately builds links that reinforce Google's confidence in your site. Buying links or participating in link schemes does the opposite. Learn more in our Content Marketing pillar . Signal Two: Content Quality, Depth, and Accuracy Google's Helpful Content System is designed to reward content that demonstrates genuine helpfulness and penalize content created primarily to rank rather than to serve readers. Google's own documentation describes the system as rewarding content that provides visitors with "a satisfying experience" and that "demonstrates first-hand expertise and a deep level of knowledge." Comprehensiveness and Depth Backlinko's analysis of search results showed that longer, more comprehensive content consistently ranks higher than thinner content for competitive keywords. The average first-page result contains significantly more words than those on page two, not simply because length alone is rewarded, but because length indicates comprehensiveness, which is what Google's systems actually evaluate.

Give First. 09 Your Analytics Are Telling You What to Do 10 The One Question That Changes Everything Most business owners treat social media like a megaphone. They broadcast products, promotions, and announcements and wonder why nobody cares. The businesses winning on social media right now aren't louder. They're smarter. They understand one thing most people miss: people don't engage with content. They engage with content that makes them feel something. Here's how to build that, systematically. The Foundation: Understand Why People Actually Engage Before tactics, you need the right mental model. Every time someone likes, comments, or shares your post, they're doing it for one of three reasons: It reflects who they are. Sharing it makes them look smart, funny, or in-the-know. It gives them something. A useful insight, a laugh, a new perspective. It makes them feel seen. You articulated something they've experienced but never said out loud. If your content doesn't hit at least one of these, no tactic will save it. Keep this filter in mind for everything that follows. On every platform, content gets cut off after one or two lines. Users see that preview before deciding to keep scrolling or tap to read more. That first line isn't a warm-up: it's a tollgate. You either get paid to continue or you don't. The best first lines do one of four things: Create a knowledge gap. "Most businesses are doing email marketing backwards." Make a counterintuitive claim. "Posting less grew our following faster." State a specific, surprising result. "We doubled revenue without a single new customer." Trigger immediate recognition. "If your social media feels like shouting into a void, here's why." Write your entire post first. Then write the first line last, knowing its only job is to make the second line impossible not to read. Vague content is invisible. "Tips for growing your business" gets scrolled past. "How we landed our first 10 enterprise clients using 15-minute voice notes instead of cold emails" gets read, saved, and shared. Specificity does two things at once: it makes your content credible because you clearly have real experience, and it makes it useful because people can actually apply it. Before publishing, ask: can I replace any general word with a specific one? You don't need to be dramatic. You need to be precise. Every major platform (Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook, TikTok, X) is designed to keep users on that platform. Any content that sends people away gets suppressed by the algorithm. Posts with external links, embedded YouTube videos, or "click the link in bio" as the main call-to-action all receive a fraction of the distribution of native content. Upload videos directly to each platform rather than linking to YouTube Write captions that deliver complete value on their own, without requiring a click If you need to share a link, put it in the first comment, not the post itself Design graphics that live on the platform and don't need context from anywhere else This one change, going native, can double or triple your organic reach without changing anything else. This pairs directly with a strong content repurposing strategy . Data doesn't go viral. Feelings do. People share content because of how it makes them feel, not because it was accurate or well-researched. Information is the vehicle. Emotion is what drives it. Before every post, ask yourself: what is the dominant emotion someone feels after reading this? If your answer is "informed," that's not enough. Aim for one of these: One emotion, clearly felt, is worth more than ten facts cleanly presented. The way most businesses write social media posts is exactly how they'd write a brochure, professional tone, company perspective, features and benefits.

An AI hallucination happens when an AI tool produces information that sounds confident and plausible but is false or made up. Examples include invented statistics, fake quotes, wrong business hours, nonexistent sources, or services a business does not offer. Hallucinations happen because language models generate likely-sounding text based on patterns, and they do not automatically verify facts. Tools that search the web or read trusted documents reduce errors, yet mistakes can still occur. Why AI Hallucinations Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Hallucinations affect businesses in two ways. First, AI-assisted marketing content can include errors that damage trust if published without review. Second, AI assistants may describe your business incorrectly, such as listing old hours or the wrong services for a Goshen salon. Clear, consistent information across your website, Google Business Profile , and directories gives AI tools accurate sources to draw from, reducing the chance of wrong answers about your business. Hallucinations also appear in research. An AI tool may produce a convincing statistic about local market size or customer behavior that has no real source behind it. Publishing such a number can undermine credibility with customers who check. How AI Hallucinations Works Pattern-based generation Models predict likely text, not verified facts. b: Resources / Glossaries / AI & Automation Glossary Large Language Model (LLM): A foundation model trained on large amounts of text to understand and generate language. LLMs power tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. What Is Large Language Model? A large language model, or LLM, is an AI system trained on enormous amounts of text to understand and generate human language. It learns patterns in how words and ideas relate, which allows it to answer questions, summarize documents, write drafts, translate, and hold conversations. A Goshen business can use LLMs to draft emails, summarize reviews, brainstorm content ideas, and answer routine questions, freeing time for customers, as long as a person reviews the results. A Middlebury bakery owner uses an LLM to draft weekly social posts, summarize customer reviews into themes, and write first drafts of holiday ordering instructions. b: Resources / Glossaries / AI & Automation Glossary Prompt Engineering: The skill of writing and refining prompts so AI tools produce accurate, useful, on-brand results. What Is Prompt Engineering? Prompt engineering is the practice of writing and refining instructions, called prompts, so AI tools produce accurate, useful, and on-brand results. It includes giving context, defining the task, setting constraints, providing examples, and specifying the format you want. It is less about secret tricks and more about clear communication. The same principles that help you brief a new employee, such as explaining the goal, the audience, and what good work looks like, also help AI tools deliver better output. Prompting is also a learnable team skill. Once a few people discover prompts that work, sharing them as templates raises the quality of everyone's AI-assisted work and keeps your brand voice consistent across emails, posts, and documents. Why Prompt Engineering Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Vague prompts produce generic results. A Goshen insurance agency that asks "Write a blog post about insurance" gets bland text, while a prompt describing its audience, local focus, tone, and key points produces a far more useful draft. Good prompts save time and reduce errors. For small teams across Northern Indiana using AI for emails, social posts, and research, a few reusable prompt templates can improve quality across everything they produce. How Prompt Engineering Works Give context Describe your business, audience, and goal. Define the task State exactly what you want produced. Set constraints Specify length, tone, words to avoid, and must-include points. Show examples Share samples of the style or format you want. Iterate Review the output and refine the prompt with feedback. A Warsaw marina's first prompt, "Write a Facebook post about boat storage," produces a generic draft. The revised prompt reads: "You are writing for a family-owned marina on Lake Wawasee. Write a friendly 80-word Facebook post reminding boat owners to reserve winter storage by October 15. Mention shrink-wrapping and indoor storage, use a warm local tone, and end with a call to book online." The result needs only light editing. The marina saves the improved prompt as a template and reuses it for seasonal reminders throughout the year. Getting Started With Prompt Engineering Write a short "business brief" you can paste into prompts: what you do, who you serve, where you operate, your tone of voice, and words to use or avoid. This context alone improves most AI output. For each common task, such as review replies, social posts, or email drafts, build a prompt template with the task, audience, length, tone, and format. Save the templates your team finds most useful, and keep refining them based on the edits you make most often. Quick Wins to Improve Your Prompts Create a reusable business brief for prompts State the audience, goal, length, and tone every time Provide an example of the style you want Ask for revisions instead of starting over Save and share your best prompt templates Missing context. AI cannot know your business details unless you provide them. Overlong prompts. Clear and organized beats long and rambling. Fact checking. Better prompts reduce errors, and review is still essential. Sensitive data. Avoid pasting private customer information into public tools. Do I need technical skills for prompt engineering? No. Clear writing and specific instructions matter most. What makes a good prompt? Context, a clear task, constraints, examples, and the output format you want. Should prompts be long or short? As long as needed to be clear. Most business prompts work well with a few organized sentences or bullet points. Can prompt templates be shared with a team? Yes. b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Click-Through Rate (CTR): The percentage of people who click after seeing your ad, search listing, or email link. What Is Click-Through Rate? Click-through rate, or CTR, measures the percentage of people who click a link after seeing it. The formula is clicks divided by impressions, multiplied by 100. If your ad is shown 1,000 times and earns 50 clicks, your CTR is 5 percent. CTR applies across marketing: search results, Google Ads , social media ads, and emails, where it usually measures clicks divided by emails delivered. Each channel has its own typical ranges, so compare results within the same channel. Why Click-Through Rate Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CTR shows whether your message stands out. A Mishawaka roofing company may appear in search results thousands of times a month, yet if few people click, that visibility produces little business. Raising CTR turns existing visibility into more visitors and leads. In Google Ads, a strong expected CTR also contributes to Quality Score , which can lower your cost per click . For Northern Indiana businesses on modest budgets, that efficiency adds up. Watching CTR over time also gives early warnings. A sudden drop often signals a new competitor, an outdated offer, or a change on the results page, giving you a chance to respond before leads decline. How Click-Through Rate Works Impressions The number of times your listing, ad, or email is shown. Clicks The number of times people click through. The calculation CTR equals clicks divided by impressions, times 100. Channel context Search, display, social, and email each have different typical CTRs. Position matters Higher placements in search usually earn higher CTR. A South Bend dental practice sees in Google Search Console that its implants page earns thousands of impressions with a CTR under 1 percent. Its title reads "Services - Smile Dental." It rewrites the title to "Dental Implants in South Bend | Free Consultation " and improves the meta description . Over the next two months, the page's CTR more than doubles at a similar average position. The practice applies the same approach to its other service pages and sees clicks grow without needing higher rankings. Getting Started With Click-Through Rate Find your CTR data in Google Search Console for organic search, Google Ads for paid search, Meta Ads Manager for social ads, and your email platform for newsletters. Note which pages, ads, or emails have high impressions but low CTR. Improve those first. For search, rewrite title tags and meta descriptions. For ads, test new headlines and offers. For email, write clearer subject lines and stronger calls to action. Change one element at a time, wait for enough data, and compare results. Quick Wins to Improve Your Click-Through Rate Rewrite titles on high-impression, low-click pages Include the service and town in search titles Test new ad headlines and offers regularly Use clear, benefit-focused email calls to action Add schema to qualify for richer search results Clicks without conversions. High CTR matters most when visitors also take action. Misleading copy. Clickbait may raise CTR while lowering trust and conversions. AI Overviews. Some searches earn fewer clicks as answers appear on the results page. Small samples. Wait for enough impressions before judging a change. It depends on the channel, industry, and position. Compare your results with your own past performance and similar campaigns. Divide clicks by impressions and multiply by 100. Google has not confirmed CTR as a direct ranking factor, yet higher CTR means more visitors from the rankings you already have. Does CTR affect Google Ads costs? Expected CTR is part of Quality Score, which influences ad rank and cost per click. Common causes include new competitors, ads or AI Overviews above your listing, ranking changes, or outdated titles. b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Conversion Rate: The percentage of visitors who take the action you want, such as calling, booking, or buying. Conversion rate is the percentage of visitors or recipients who complete a desired action, such as submitting a form, calling, booking an appointment, or making a purchase. The formula is conversions divided by total visitors (or clicks), multiplied by 100. If 1,000 people visit your website in a month and 30 request a quote, your conversion rate is 3 percent. You can measure it for the whole site, for individual pages, or for specific campaigns. Why Conversion Rate Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Conversion rate turns traffic into revenue. A Goshen HVAC company that raises its website conversion rate from 2 to 4 percent doubles its leads without spending another dollar on traffic. It also reveals where marketing is working. Comparing conversion rates by page, channel, and campaign shows which messages and offers resonate with customers across Northern Indiana and Michiana . Even small gains compound. A one-point improvement on a page that receives steady traffic every month adds up to many extra calls and bookings over a year, all from visitors you were already attracting. Track it Use Google Analytics 4 , ad platforms, and call tracking to record each conversion. Calculate Conversions divided by visitors, times 100. Compare segments Look at rates by page, device, channel, and campaign. Test improvements Change headlines, offers, forms, and layouts, then measure. A Plymouth med spa receives steady website traffic, but few visitors book. It shortens its booking form from twelve fields to four, adds before-and-after photos, displays its Google rating near the booking button, and adds a click-to-call button on mobile. Its booking page conversion rate rises noticeably over the following two months. The spa also learns that mobile visitors convert better by calling, so it makes the phone button more prominent on mobile layouts. Getting Started With Conversion Rate Set up conversion tracking for your most valuable actions, including calls, forms, and bookings. Then find your current conversion rate for the whole site and for your top landing pages in Google Analytics 4. Pick the page with the most traffic and the lowest conversion rate. It varies widely by industry, offer, and traffic source. Compare your pages with your own past results and improve steadily. How do I calculate conversion rate? b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Cost Per Click (CPC): The average amount you pay each time someone clicks your ad. Cost per click, or CPC, is the amount an advertiser pays each time someone clicks an ad. Average CPC equals total ad cost divided by total clicks. If you spend $500 and receive 250 clicks, your average CPC is $2. On Google Ads and Microsoft Ads, CPC is set through an auction each time someone searches. Your bid, your ad's quality, and the competition determine your position and price. Social platforms such as Meta often charge by impressions but report CPC as well. Why Cost Per Click Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CPC determines how much traffic your budget can buy. A Valparaiso personal injury law firm may face high CPCs because competition is intense, while a Goshen pet groomer may pay much less. Understanding CPC helps you set realistic budgets and expectations. CPC also connects directly to results. Dividing your cost per lead by your cost per click shows how many clicks it takes to earn a lead, which tells you whether to focus on cheaper traffic or on landing pages that convert more of the clicks you already pay for. Lower CPC means more clicks for the same spend. Improving ad relevance and landing pages can bring CPC down while keeping your ads in strong positions. Auction Advertisers compete each time a relevant search happens. Bid The most you are willing to pay for a click. Quality Expected CTR , ad relevance, and landing page experience influence ad rank . Ad rank Bid, quality, and other factors decide your position. Actual CPC You often pay less than your maximum bid, based on the competition. A Goshen dental office pays a high CPC for broad keywords such as "dentist." It shifts budget to more specific searches such as "emergency dentist Goshen" and "dental implants Elkhart County ," writes tightly matched ads, and builds dedicated landing pages. Its Quality Scores rise, average CPC falls, and more clicks turn into appointments. The office also adds negative keywords such as "jobs" and "school" so its budget stays focused on patients. Getting Started With Cost Per Click Open your Google Ads Keywords report and sort by cost. Look at average CPC, conversions, and Quality Score for your most expensive keywords to see which ones earn their price. Focus budget on keywords with strong conversion rates, pause or lower bids on expensive keywords that rarely convert, and add negative keywords to block irrelevant searches. Improve ads and landing pages for your core keywords to raise Quality Score, then track how average CPC and cost per lead change. Broad keywords can attract costly, unrelated searches without negatives. Bid wars. Raising bids without improving quality often just raises costs. It depends on your industry and the value of a customer. Judge CPC alongside conversion rate and cost per lead. Why are some keywords so expensive? Highly competitive, high-value searches attract many advertisers, which raises prices. Improve Quality Score, use specific keywords, add negatives, and target your service area precisely. Often not. b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Cost Per Lead (CPL): What each new inquiry costs you, such as a call, form, or booking request. Cost per lead, or CPL, measures how much marketing spend it takes to generate one new lead, such as a call, form submission, or booking request. The formula is total marketing spend divided by the number of leads. If you spend $1,500 on Google Ads in a month and receive 30 qualified leads, your CPL is $50. You can calculate CPL by channel, campaign, or service to see where leads come most efficiently. Why Cost Per Lead Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CPL helps small businesses compare channels on equal terms. A Goshen remodeler may find that Google search leads cost more each than Facebook leads, yet close at a much higher rate, which makes search the better investment. Tracking CPL over time also shows whether improvements are working. Better ads, landing pages, and targeting should steadily lower the cost of each lead. CPL also makes budget conversations easier. When you know a lead costs about $50 and roughly one in four becomes a customer, you can plan exactly how much spend it takes to fill next month's schedule. d: Customer acquisition cost is the total cost of winning one new customer. Learn how to calculate CAC and how local businesses use it to guide growth.
h: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) The total cost of winning one new paying customer | What Is Customer Acquisition Cost? | Why Customer Acquisition Cost Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses | How Customer Acquisition Cost Works | A Local Example | Getting Started With Customer Acquisition Cost | Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Acquisition Cost | What to Watch For | Customer Acquisition Cost FAQ
b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC): The total cost to win one new customer, including ads, marketing tools, agency fees, and sales time. CAC is broader than cost per acquisition because it counts every cost, not just ad spend. What Is Customer Acquisition Cost? Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is the total amount you spend on marketing and sales to win one new customer. The basic formula is total acquisition costs divided by the number of new customers in the same period. If you spend $6,000 on marketing and sales in a quarter and gain 40 new customers, your CAC is $150. A full calculation can include ad spend, agency or staff costs, software, and sales time. Why Customer Acquisition Cost Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CAC shows whether growth is profitable. A Warsaw HVAC company that spends $400 to win a customer who brings in thousands of dollars over many years is growing well, while spending more than a customer is worth signals a problem. Knowing CAC also helps you decide how much to invest. When you understand what a new customer costs, you can plan budgets with confidence and compare channels on the cost of real customers rather than clicks or leads. How Customer Acquisition Cost Works Gather costs Add marketing spend, sales costs, tools, and agency fees for a period. Count new customers Use customers won in the same period. Divide Total costs divided by new customers. Break it down Calculate CAC by channel or campaign when tracking allows. Compare with value Weigh CAC against customer lifetime value . A Goshen IT services company calculates its CAC for the year and finds it spends about $1,200 to win each new managed services client. Each client stays for several years on a monthly contract, so the company decides it can afford to invest more in marketing. Breaking CAC down by channel shows referrals and LinkedIn bring the lowest CAC, so the company adds a structured referral program and expands its LinkedIn content. Getting Started With Customer Acquisition Cost Choose a period, such as the last quarter or year, and total all marketing and sales costs: ad spend, agency fees, software, and a share of staff time spent on sales and marketing. Count the new customers won in that period, then divide. If your CRM tracks lead sources, calculate CAC by channel as well. Compare CAC with the average value of a customer, and review it every quarter to see whether your marketing is becoming more efficient. Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Acquisition Cost Track lead source for every new customer Follow up with leads quickly to raise close rates Build a referral program for happy customers Invest more in channels with the lowest CAC Compare CAC with customer lifetime value Partial costs. Leaving out sales time or tools makes CAC look lower than it is. Long sales cycles. Customers may close in a later period than the spending that won them. Repeat customers. Count only new customers in CAC. Averages hide detail. CAC by channel reveals where to invest. Customer Acquisition Cost FAQ A healthy CAC is well below the value a customer brings over time. Many businesses aim for lifetime value several times higher than CAC. How is CAC different from cost per lead? Cost per lead measures the cost to generate an inquiry. CAC measures the cost to win a paying customer. Improve close rates, focus on efficient channels, encourage referrals, and nurture leads who are not ready yet. Should CAC include salaries? For a complete picture, include the share of salaries spent on marketing and sales. How often should I calculate CAC? Quarterly is a practical rhythm for most small businesses. Want to know exactly what each new customer costs and how to lower it? Riley will calculate your CAC and find the most efficient channels.

t: What Is Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)? How to Calculate It
d: Customer lifetime value is the total revenue or profit a customer brings over the whole relationship. Learn how to calculate CLV and use it to guide marketing.
h: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) The total value a customer brings over your entire relationship | What Is Customer Lifetime Value? | Why Customer Lifetime Value Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses | How Customer Lifetime Value Works | A Local Example | Getting Started With Customer Lifetime Value | Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Lifetime Value | What to Watch For | Customer Lifetime Value FAQ
b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Customer Lifetime Value (CLV): The total revenue one customer brings your business across the whole relationship. CLV tells you how much a new customer is truly worth. What Is Customer Lifetime Value? Customer lifetime value, also called CLV, CLTV, or LTV, estimates the total revenue or profit a customer brings to your business over the entire relationship. A simple formula is average purchase value, times purchases per year, times the average number of years a customer stays. If a Mishawaka auto shop customer spends $250 per visit, visits three times a year, and stays for five years, their lifetime value is about $3,750 in revenue. Using profit margin instead of revenue gives a more conservative figure. Why Customer Lifetime Value Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CLV shows how much a customer is truly worth, which changes how much you can afford to spend to win one. A Goshen dentist who knows a family stays for many years can invest confidently in marketing that brings in new families. It also highlights the value of retention. Keeping customers longer and encouraging repeat visits raises CLV, often at a far lower cost than finding new customers. CLV also helps you decide which customers to focus on. When you see that commercial accounts or service plan members stay far longer than one-time buyers, you can shape offers and marketing to attract more customers like them. How Customer Lifetime Value Works Average purchase value Total revenue divided by number of purchases. Purchase frequency How often a typical customer buys each year. Customer lifespan How many years a typical customer stays. Multiply Value times frequency times lifespan. Adjust for margin Use gross margin for a profit-based CLV. A Goshen pest control company calculates that a typical quarterly-service customer pays about $500 per year and stays for six years, for a lifetime value of about $3,000. Knowing this, the owner is comfortable spending well over the price of a first visit to win each new contract customer. The company also launches a reminder and loyalty program to keep customers longer, raising CLV across its customer base. Getting Started With Customer Lifetime Value Pull a year of sales data and calculate your average purchase value and how often customers buy. Estimate how long a typical customer stays, using your CRM or customer records. Multiply those numbers to estimate CLV, then compare it with customer acquisition cost . Look for ways to raise CLV, such as service plans, reminders, loyalty programs, and helpful follow-up emails, and recalculate once a year. Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Lifetime Value Offer service plans or memberships Send timely reminders for repeat services Follow up after each purchase with helpful tips Reward referrals and loyalty Compare CLV with CAC to guide marketing spend Optimistic estimates. Use realistic retention figures based on actual data. Revenue versus profit. Profit-based CLV gives safer spending limits. Segment differences. Different customer groups often have very different CLV. New businesses. Limited history makes early CLV estimates rough. Customer Lifetime Value FAQ What is a good CLV to CAC ratio? Many businesses aim for lifetime value at least three times acquisition cost, though the right ratio depends on margins and growth plans. How do I raise customer lifetime value? Improve retention, encourage repeat purchases, offer service plans, and build loyalty through great service and helpful communication. Should I use revenue or profit? Profit-based CLV is more conservative and better for setting spending limits. Can email marketing raise CLV? Yes. Reminders, tips, and offers keep customers coming back. Does CLV matter for one-time services? Yes. Even one-time customers bring referrals and reviews, and many businesses discover related services those customers would happily buy again. How often should I calculate CLV? Once or twice

t: What Is Return on Ad Spend (ROAS)? How to Calculate It
d: Return on ad spend measures the revenue earned for every dollar spent on ads. Learn how to calculate ROAS, set targets, and improve it.
h: Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) The revenue you earn for every dollar you spend on ads | What Is Return on Ad Spend? | Why Return on Ad Spend Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses | How Return on Ad Spend Works | A Local Example | Getting Started With Return on Ad Spend | Quick Wins to Improve Your Return on Ad Spend | What to Watch For | Return on Ad Spend FAQ
b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Return on Ad Spend (ROAS): The revenue you earn for every dollar you spend on ads. ROAS shows how hard your ad budget is working. What Is Return on Ad Spend? Return on ad spend, or ROAS, measures how much revenue your advertising generates for each dollar spent. The formula is revenue from ads divided by ad spend. If $1,000 in ads produces $5,000 in sales, your ROAS is 5, often written as 5:1 or 500 percent. ROAS focuses only on advertising costs and the revenue those ads produce. It is narrower than return on investment , which accounts for all costs, including products, labor, and overhead. Why Return on Ad Spend Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses ROAS shows which ads truly pay off. A Goshen furniture store may find that Google Shopping ads return 8 dollars for every dollar while a broad display campaign returns 1.5, which makes the next budget decision clear. For service businesses across Northern Indiana , ROAS connects ad spending to booked jobs and contracts, as long as leads are tracked through to revenue in a CRM or sales records. ROAS also keeps budgets honest during busy seasons. When demand rises and ad costs climb, comparing ROAS week over week shows whether higher spending is still producing profitable sales or simply buying more expensive clicks. How Return on Ad Spend Works Track revenue Connect ad conversions to actual sales values. Track spend Record total ad spend for the same period and campaign. Calculate Revenue divided by ad spend. Compare campaigns Find which campaigns and channels earn the highest return. Set a target Use your margins to determine the minimum profitable ROAS. A Valparaiso landscaping company spends $3,000 on Google Ads over a spring season. By tracking which leads become signed projects in its CRM, it attributes $24,000 in revenue to the ads, for a ROAS of 8. Patio and hardscape campaigns show the highest return, while general lawn care campaigns return less. The company shifts budget toward hardscape campaigns the following spring and keeps a smaller lawn care campaign focused on its best towns. Getting Started With Return on Ad Spend Make sure you can connect ad leads to revenue. For online sales, ecommerce tracking handles this. For service businesses, record the lead source in your CRM and note the value of each closed job. Calculate ROAS for each campaign over a meaningful period, such as a quarter. Then figure out your break-even ROAS using your profit margin: if your margin is 40 percent, you need a ROAS of at least 2.5 to cover ad costs. Shift budget toward campaigns comfortably above that line. Quick Wins to Improve Your Return on Ad Spend Connect ad leads to closed revenue in your CRM Calculate break-even ROAS using your profit margin Compare ROAS by campaign and channel Shift budget toward the highest-return campaigns Use Target ROAS bidding once you have enough data Revenue versus profit. A high ROAS on low-margin products may still lose money. Long sales cycles. Revenue may arrive months after the ad spend. Attribution. Customers often see several touchpoints before buying. Missing offline sales. Phone and in-person sales need tracking too. It depends on your margins. A business with high margins can profit at a lower ROAS than one with thin margins. How is ROAS different from ROI? ROAS measures revenue against ad spend. ROI measures profit against total investment. How do I calculate break-even ROAS? Divide 1 by your profit margin. A 25 percent margin requires a ROAS of 4 to break even. Can service businesses use ROAS? Yes, by tracking which ad leads become paying customers and their value. b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Return on Investment (ROI): How much profit an investment returns compared with what it cost. ROI is the clearest way to judge whether marketing is paying for itself. What Is Return on Investment? Return on investment, or ROI, measures the profit an investment produces compared with its cost. The formula is (gain from the investment minus cost) divided by cost, times 100. If marketing costing $5,000 produces $15,000 in profit, ROI is 200 percent. Marketing ROI looks at the full picture: ad spend, agency fees, software, content, and staff time on one side, and the profit from new and returning customers on the other. Why Return on Investment Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses ROI answers the question every owner asks: is marketing paying for itself? A Goshen accounting firm that knows its SEO investment returns several times its cost can invest with confidence instead of treating marketing as an expense to cut. ROI also helps compare very different investments, such as SEO, paid ads, email marketing , and a new website, on equal terms, guiding budget decisions for Northern Indiana businesses. Knowing your ROI also changes conversations with partners, lenders, and staff. Instead of debating whether marketing "works," you can point to clear numbers showing what each channel returned and plan next year's growth with confidence. How Return on Investment Works Total the costs Include ad spend, fees, tools, and time. Measure the gain Use profit, not just revenue, from customers the marketing produced. Calculate Gain minus cost, divided by cost, times 100. Consider timing Some channels, such as SEO, build returns over months and years. Compare channels Look at ROI by channel to guide future investment. A Warsaw HVAC company invests $18,000 in a year of SEO, Google Ads , and email marketing. Its CRM shows those channels produced customers generating $95,000 in revenue at a 40 percent gross margin, or $38,000 in gross profit. ROI is ($38,000 minus $18,000) divided by $18,000, or about 111 percent. Breaking ROI down by channel reveals email marketing to past customers delivers the highest return, so the company expands its maintenance reminder program. Getting Started With Return on Investment Track lead sources for every new customer in a CRM or simple spreadsheet. Without knowing where customers come from, ROI becomes guesswork. Add up all marketing costs for a period, then total the profit from customers those efforts produced. Calculate ROI overall and by channel. Remember that SEO and content often keep producing customers long after the work is done, so review ROI over a full year as well as month to month. Customers often interact with several channels before buying. What is a good marketing ROI? Any positive ROI means marketing returns more than it costs. Many businesses aim for several dollars of profit for every dollar spent. How is ROI different from ROAS? ROI measures profit against total cost. ROAS measures revenue against ad spend only. How do I measure ROI for SEO? Track organic leads and customers over time, and compare their profit with the cost of SEO. Should ROI include customer lifetime value? b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing KPIs Glossary Review Velocity: How many new reviews your business earns in a set period. A steady flow shows customers and search engines that you are active and trusted. Review velocity is the rate at which a business earns new online reviews over time, such as six new Google reviews a month. It looks at the flow of reviews, not just the total count or average rating. Steady velocity shows that real customers keep choosing and talking about your business. A company with 200 reviews but none in the past year looks less active than a competitor with 80 reviews and several new ones every week. Why Review Velocity Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Customers notice dates. A Warsaw homeowner comparing contractors trusts recent reviews more than ones from several years ago, because they describe the business as it operates today. Reviews are also a key part of local search prominence, and recency and steady activity help Google and AI tools see your business as established and trusted across Northern Indiana and Michiana . How Review Velocity Works Total review count The number of reviews you have accumulated. Recency How recently customers left reviews. Steady flow A consistent pace over months, rather than one large burst. Rating and content The average rating and the details customers mention, such as services and towns. Owner responses Thoughtful replies show the business listens. A Goshen auto repair shop has 140 Google reviews, but the newest is ten months old. Getting Started With Review Velocity Choose the moment when customers are happiest, usually right after a job is completed or a purchase is picked up. Train your team to mention reviews in person, add the link to receipts and follow-up emails, and reply to every review within a few days. Track new reviews each month to keep the pace steady. How many reviews should I get per month? Aim for a steady pace that matches or exceeds top local competitors in your category. Do review replies help rankings? Replies show engagement and build customer trust, and Google encourages businesses to respond. Can I ask customers for reviews? Yes. Google allows businesses to ask for reviews, as long as there are no incentives and every customer is asked fairly. What should I do about a negative review? Alt text, short for alternative text, is a written description of an image added in the page code. Good alt text describes what matters about the image in the context of the page. Purely decorative images, such as background shapes, use empty alt text so screen readers skip them. Accessibility is also part of a professional, trustworthy online presence. Alt text supports SEO too. It helps your project photos appear in Google Images and gives search engines more context about each page, which matters for businesses whose work is visual, such as remodelers, landscapers, salons, and restaurants across Michiana . Describe the content State what the image shows that matters to the reader. Add useful context Include details such as the service or location when they are genuinely relevant. Keep it concise A sentence or short phrase usually works best. Skip "image of" Screen readers already announce images. Leave decorative images empty Use an empty alt attribute for images that add no information. A Middlebury kitchen remodeler's gallery has fifty photos named "IMG_4021.jpg" with no alt text. It adds descriptions such as "white shaker kitchen cabinets with quartz countertops in a Middlebury farmhouse remodel." The gallery becomes usable for screen reader visitors, and several photos begin appearing in Google Images searches for kitchen remodel ideas in Northern Indiana . Getting Started With Alt Text Audit your most visited pages first: homepage, top service pages, and gallery or portfolio pages. Many website builders show the alt text field when you click an image in the editor, and free accessibility checkers can list every image missing alt text. Write descriptions the way you would explain the photo to someone over the phone. Focus on what the image shows and why it is on the page. Rename new image files with descriptive words before uploading, and make writing alt text part of your routine every time you add a photo, so your site stays accessible as it grows. Quick Wins to Improve Your Alt Text Add alt text to every meaningful image on key pages Describe project photos with the service and setting Use empty alt text for decorative graphics Rename image files with descriptive words before uploading Describe text inside images, such as logos or charts Keyword stuffing. Lists of keywords harm accessibility and add no SEO value. Missing context. Describe what matters about the image on that specific page. Image-only text. Important information should also appear as real text on the page. Linked images. When an image is a link, its alt text should describe the destination. Alt text is a core part of web accessibility standards such as WCAG, and it is strongly recommended for every meaningful image. How long should alt text be? Usually one short sentence. Complex charts can be summarized in alt text and explained in more detail on the page. Yes. It helps search engines understand images and supports visibility in image search. Search engines read anchor text as a description of the linked page. Anchors appear both on your own site, through internal links, and on other websites that link to you, through backlinks. It also tells Google that your linked page is about that topic, strengthening its relevance for related searches. Descriptive anchors Words that describe the destination, such as "AC repair." Branded anchors Your business name, often used by other sites linking to you. Partial match anchors Phrases that include the topic naturally, such as "tips from our HVAC team." Generic anchors Phrases like "read more" that offer little context. Naked URLs The web address itself used as the link. A Kokomo law firm's blog posts end with "Contact us here" links. Visitors click through more often, and the practice area pages gain stronger relevance for estate planning searches in the region. Getting Started With Anchor Text Review the links inside your blog posts and service pages. Repeating one exact keyword in many backlinks can look manipulative. Misleading anchors. Anchors should accurately describe where the link goes. Accessibility. Screen reader users often scan links alone, so descriptive anchors help them navigate. Image links. When an image is a link, its alt text acts as the anchor. Does anchor text still matter for SEO? Yes. It remains a helpful signal for what a linked page covers, especially for internal links you control. Should I ask other sites to use keywords in links? A business name or natural phrase is usually best. Natural variety reads as more trustworthy. What is exact match anchor text? An anchor that uses the precise keyword a page targets. Use it occasionally among more natural variations. How is anchor text different from alt text? Anchor text is the clickable wording of a text link. Alt text describes an image, and when that image is a link, its alt text serves as the anchor. Does anchor text help accessibility? Yes. Google's original ranking system was built on links, and they remain one of the clearest signals of authority, alongside content quality and relevance. Personas also make decisions faster. Research real customers Interview customers, review sales notes, and study reviews. Find patterns Group shared goals, challenges, questions, and objections. Write the profile Summarize demographics, goals, pain points, and decision factors. Map their journey Note where they search, what they compare, and what convinces them. Apply everywhere Use personas to guide content, ads, offers, and sales conversations. Outdated profiles. Refresh personas as your customers evolve. How many buyer personas should I have? Most small businesses do well with two to four personas based on their main customer groups. t: What Is a Call to Action? Writing CTAs That Get Results
d: A call to action tells visitors exactly what to do next, such as call, book, or get a quote. Learn how to write and place CTAs that turn visitors into customers.
h: Call to Action (CTA) The clear next step that turns interest into action | What Is Call to Action? | Why Call to Action Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses | How Call to Action Works | A Local Example | Getting Started With Call to Action | Quick Wins to Improve Your Calls to Action | What to Watch For | Call to Action FAQ
b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing Terms Glossary Call to Action (CTA): A button or phrase that invites the visitor to take the next step, such as calling, booking, or requesting a quote. Every important page benefits from one clear CTA. A call to action, or CTA, is a prompt that invites someone to take a specific next step, such as "Book a Free Consultation ," "Get a Quote," "Call Now," or "Download the Guide." CTAs appear as buttons, links, and lines of copy on websites, emails, ads, social posts, and printed materials. A strong CTA is clear, specific, and tied to what the reader wants. It tells people exactly what will happen when they act and why that step helps them. Why Call to Action Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Visitors to a local business website usually have a goal: get a price, check availability, or talk to someone. A Mishawaka electrician whose pages end with "Request a Same-Day Estimate" makes that goal easy to reach, while a page with no clear next step leaves visitors to find the phone number on their own. Better CTAs often raise conversions without any increase in traffic, which makes them one of the most cost-effective improvements for Northern Indiana businesses. Start with an action verb Book, call, get, schedule, compare, or download. Name the benefit "Get Your Free Estimate" says more than "Submit." Make it visible Use contrasting buttons placed where people decide. Match the stage Early visitors may want a guide, while ready buyers want to book. Reduce friction Short forms and click-to-call buttons make acting easy. A Goshen tree service's website uses a single "Contact Us" link at the bottom of each page. It adds a "Get a Free Tree Removal Estimate" button near the top of each service page, a click-to-call button on mobile, and a short form asking only for name, phone, and town. Estimate requests increase in the following months with the same website traffic. The company also adds a softer CTA, "See Our Storm Cleanup Checklist," for visitors who are researching rather than ready to call. Getting Started With Call to Action Review your homepage and top service pages on a phone. Within the first screen, can a visitor see what you offer and one clear next step? If not, add a primary CTA button near the top of each page. Rewrite vague CTAs such as "Submit" or "Learn More" to describe the result, such as "Get My Free Quote." Use one primary CTA per page, repeat it after key sections, and keep forms short. Track clicks and conversions, then test new wording on your highest-traffic page. Quick Wins to Improve Your Calls to Action Place a clear CTA button near the top of each key page Use specific, benefit-focused button text Add click-to-call buttons for mobile visitors Shorten forms to only the details you need Offer a softer CTA for early researchers Too many choices. Several competing CTAs can stall decisions; lead with one. Vague wording. "Submit" and "Click Here" give no reason to act. Mismatch. The page after the click should deliver exactly what the CTA promised. Accessibility. Buttons need readable contrast and large tap targets. Where should a CTA go on a page? Near the top, after key sections, and at the end, so visitors can act whenever they are ready. How many CTAs should a page have? One primary action, repeated where helpful, with an optional secondary action for early researchers. What makes a CTA effective? A clear action verb, a specific benefit, and an easy next step. What is the difference between a primary and secondary CTA? A primary CTA is the main action you want, such as booking or calling. A secondary CTA offers a lighter step, such as reading a guide, for visitors who are still deciding. Should every email have a CTA? Yes. Each email should guide readers to one clear next step. Rules vary by state, and some states require consent from everyone on the call. Many businesses play a short recording announcement at the start of each call. t: What Is a Canonical URL? Preventing Duplicate Content
d: A canonical URL tells search engines which version of a page is the main one. Learn how canonical tags prevent duplicate content and consolidate ranking signals.

b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing Terms Glossary Canonical URL: A tag that names the preferred version of a page when similar versions exist, so search engines credit one main address. A canonical URL is the main version of a page that you want search engines to index and show in results. It is usually declared with a canonical tag, a short line in the page code that points to the preferred address. Websites often create several addresses for the same content without anyone noticing: versions with and without "www," tracking parameters added by ads or emails, filtered product pages, and printer-friendly copies. The canonical tag tells search engines which one counts. Why Canonical URL Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses When search engines find the same content at several addresses, they must guess which to rank, and ranking signals such as links can split between versions. A clear canonical keeps your Elkhart service page's strength focused on one address. Canonical URLs also keep reporting clean. Google Search Console data, analytics, and AI citations all point to the same page, making it easier to measure what each page earns. One preferred address Choose the URL you want indexed, usually the clean version without parameters. Self-referencing tags Each main page includes a canonical tag pointing to itself. Duplicates point to the original Variations include a canonical tag pointing to the preferred version. Consistent signals Internal links, sitemaps, and redirects all use the canonical address. Google decides Canonicals are strong hints, and Google chooses the final version based on all signals. A Granger furniture store's product pages appear under several addresses because shoppers can sort by color and price. Google indexes many near-identical versions, and none rank well. After adding canonical tags that point each variation to the main product page and updating the sitemap , the main pages become the indexed versions and their rankings improve. Its Search Console reports also become easier to read. Clicks and impressions that were scattered across dozens of filtered addresses now roll up to one page per product, so the owner can finally see which furniture lines attract the most search interest. Getting Started With Canonical URL Open the Pages report under Indexing in Google Search Console. Look for statuses such as "Duplicate without user-selected canonical" or "Alternate page with proper canonical tag." These tell you where Google sees duplicate versions and which version it chose. Next, confirm that every main page includes a self-referencing canonical tag with the full, final address, including https and your preferred www setting. Most website platforms and SEO plugins add these automatically, so check that the setting is on. Redirect old or alternate versions where possible, and make sure your sitemap and internal links use only canonical addresses. Quick Wins to Improve Your Canonical Setup Add a self-referencing canonical tag to every main page Use one consistent address format with https Point filtered or parameter versions to the main page List only canonical URLs in your sitemap Redirect old page versions to their current address Conflicting signals. Canonicals that disagree with redirects or sitemaps confuse search engines. Wrong targets. Pointing a page to an unrelated canonical can remove it from search. Relative paths. Use full URLs in canonical tags to avoid mistakes. Redesigns and migrations. Recheck canonical tags after any site rebuild. Is a canonical tag the same as a redirect? No. A redirect sends visitors and search engines to a new address. A canonical tag keeps both pages accessible while telling search engines which to index. Do I need canonical tags on a small site? Yes. Even small sites create duplicate addresses through tracking links and platform settings, and self-referencing canonicals prevent confusion. Will Google always follow my canonical? Conversion tracking is the process of recording when a visitor takes a valuable action, such as calling your business, submitting a quote request, booking an appointment, or making a purchase. t: What Are Core Web Vitals? Page Speed Metrics Explained
d: Core Web Vitals are Google's measurements of loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Learn LCP, INP, and CLS, their targets, and how faster sites win more customers.
h: Core Web Vitals Google's measurements of how fast, responsive, and stable your pages feel | What Is Core Web Vitals? | Why Core Web Vitals Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses | How Core Web Vitals Works | A Local Example | Getting Started With Core Web Vitals | Quick Wins to Improve Your Core Web Vitals | What to Watch For | Core Web Vitals FAQ
b: Resources / Glossaries / Marketing Terms Glossary Core Web Vitals: Google's measurements of how fast a page loads, how quickly it responds to taps, and how steady the layout stays while loading. Strong scores create a smoother visit and support better rankings. Core Web Vitals are three measurements Google uses to describe real visitors' experience on a page. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness to taps and clicks, and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures how much the layout jumps while loading. Google's "good" thresholds are an LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, an INP of 200 milliseconds or less, and a CLS of 0.1 or less, measured across real visits. These scores appear in Google Search Console and PageSpeed Insights. Why Core Web Vitals Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Most local searches happen on phones, often on cellular connections in parking lots or job sites. A Valparaiso customer who waits on a slow page or taps a button that jumps away is likely to go back and choose a faster competitor. Page experience is part of how Google evaluates pages, and fast pages also convert better. Improving Core Web Vitals helps rankings, ad landing pages, and leads at the same time. How Core Web Vitals Works Largest Contentful Paint How quickly the biggest visible element, often a hero image or headline, finishes loading. Interaction to Next Paint How quickly the page responds visually after a visitor taps, clicks, or types. Cumulative Layout Shift How much content moves unexpectedly as images, fonts, and ads load. Field data Google uses data from real Chrome users over the past 28 days, so improvements show up gradually. A Warsaw boutique's homepage hero image is a 4 MB photo, and its LCP sits around five seconds on phones. After compressing images, serving modern formats, reserving space for the banner, and removing an unused slider script, the page loads in under two seconds and the shop sees more product page visits from mobile searchers. Getting Started With Core Web Vitals Open Google Search Console and review the Core Web Vitals report for both mobile and desktop. It groups pages as Good, Needs Improvement, or Poor and names the metric holding each group back. Then run your most important pages, usually the homepage and top service pages, through PageSpeed Insights to see specific recommendations. Fix the largest issues first. Oversized images are the most common cause of slow loading, so resize and compress them before anything else. Reserve space for images and banners so content stays steady, and remove scripts or plugins that no longer earn their place. Mailbox providers such as Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook, and Apple decide where each email goes based on your sender reputation, domain authentication, engagement, list quality, and content.
